======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Datar–Mathews method
======================================================================

The '''Datar–Mathews Method'''<ref name="DM2007">{{cite journal |last1=Mathews |first1=Scott |last2=Datar |first2=Vinay |last3=Johnson |first3=Blake |year=2007 |title=A Practical Method for Valuing Real Options: The Boeing Approach |journal=Journal of Applied Corporate Finance |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=95–104 |doi=10.1111/j.1745-6622.2007.00140.x }}</ref> ('''DM Method''')<ref>U.S. Patent No. 6,862,579 (issued March 1, 2005).</ref> is a method for [[real options valuation]]. The method provides an easy way to determine the real option value of a project simply by using the average of positive outcomes for the project. The method can be understood as an extension of the [[net present value]] (NPV) multi-scenario [[Monte Carlo model]] with an adjustment for [[risk aversion]] and economic decision-making. The method uses information that arises naturally in a standard [[discounted cash flow]] (DCF), or [[Net present value|NPV]], project financial valuation. It was created in 2000 by Vinay Datar, professor at [[Seattle University]]; and Scott H. Mathews, [[Boeing Technical Fellowship|Technical Fellow]] at [[The Boeing Company]].

== Method ==
[[File:Datar_Mathews_Real_Option_Method_Wikipedia_Fig_1_Typical_Project_Cash_Flow_with_Uncertainty.jpg|right|thumb|Fig. 1 Typical project cash flow with uncertainty]]
The mathematical equation for the DM Method is shown below. The method captures the real option value by discounting the [[Probability distribution|distribution]] of [[operating profit]]s at ''R'', the [[market risk]] rate, and discounting the distribution of the discretionary investment at ''r'', [[risk-free rate]], ''before'' the expected payoff is calculated. The option value is then the expected value of the maximum of the difference between the two discounted distributions or zero.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nugroho |first1=Lukito Adi |last2=McMillan |first2=David |title=Real options valuation of franchise territorial exclusivity |journal=Cogent Business & Management |date=28 April 2017 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=4–5 |doi=10.1080/23311975.2016.1262490|doi-access=free |hdl=10419/205932 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite conference |url=http://realoptions.org/papers2010/106.pdf |title=Reconciling Real Option Models: An Approach to Incorporate Market and Private Uncertainties |last1= Barton|first1=Kelsey |last2=Lawryshyn |first2=Yuri |date=2010-06-17 |location=Rome, Italy |conference=Real Options: Theory Meets Practice - 14th Annual International Conference}}</ref> Fig. 1.

: <math>C_0 = E \left[\max\left(\tilde S_Te^{-Rt}-\tilde X_Te^{-rt},0\right)\right]</math>

* <math>\tilde S_T</math> is a [[random variable]] representing the future benefits, or operating profits at time ''T''. The [[Present value|present valuation]] of <math>\tilde S_T</math> uses ''R'', a discount rate consistent with the risk level of <math>\tilde S_T,</math> <math>\tilde S_0=\tilde S_Te^{-RT}.</math> ''R'' is the [[required rate of return]] for participation in the target market, sometimes termed the [[Minimum acceptable rate of return|hurdle rate]].
* <math>\tilde X_T</math> is a random variable representing the [[strike price]]. The present valuation of <math>\tilde X_T</math> uses ''r'', the rate consistent with the risk of capital investment of <math>\tilde X_T,</math> <math>\tilde X_0=\tilde X_Te^{-rT}.</math> In many generalized option applications, the risk-free discount rate is used. However other discount rates can be considered, such as the corporate bond rate, particularly when the application is an internal corporate product development project.
* <math>C_0</math> is the real option value for a single stage project. The option value can be understood as the expected value of the difference of two present value distributions with an economically rational threshold limiting losses on a risk-adjusted basis. This value may also be expressed as a stochastic distribution.

The differential discount rate for ''R'' and ''r'' implicitly allows the DM Method to account for the underlying risk.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Savolainen |first1=Jyrki |author2=Collan, Mikael |author3=Luukka, Pasi |title=Combining System Dynamic Modeling and the Datar–Mathews Method for Analyzing Metal Mine Investments |journal=Acta Universitatis Palackianae Olomucensis. Facultas Rerum Naturalium. Mathematica |date=2016 |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=95–110 |issn=0231-9721|hdl=10338.dmlcz/145821 }}</ref> If ''R'' > ''r'', then the option will be [[risk-averse]], typical for both financial and real options. If ''R'' < ''r'', then the option will be risk-seeking. If ''R'' = ''r'', then this is termed a [[risk-neutral]] option, and has parallels with NPV-type analyses with decision-making, such as [[decision tree]]s. The DM Method gives the same results as the [[Black–Scholes]] and the [[Binomial options pricing model|binomial lattice]] option models, provided the same inputs and the discount methods are used. This non-traded real option value therefore is dependent on the [[risk perception]] of the evaluator toward a market asset relative to a privately held investment asset.

The DM Method is advantageous for use in real option applications because unlike some other option models it does not require a value for ''sigma'' (a measure of uncertainty) or for ''S<sub>0</sub>'' (the value of the project today), both of which are difficult to derive for new product development projects; see [[Real options valuation#Technical considerations|further]] under [[real options valuation]]. Finally, the DM Method uses real-world values of [[List of probability distributions|any distribution type]], avoiding the requirement for conversion to risk-neutral values and the restriction of a [[lognormal distribution]];<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Datar |first1=Vinay T. |last2=Mathews |first2=Scott H. |year=2004 |ssrn=560982 |title=European Real Options: An Intuitive Algorithm for the Black–Scholes Formula}}</ref> see [[Monte Carlo methods for option pricing#Application|further]] under [[Monte Carlo methods for option pricing]]. [[File:Datar-Mathews versus Black-Scholes Methods V2.webm|thumb|Simulation demonstration of a real option calculation by Datar-Mathews Method compared with static option calculation by Black-Scholes Method]]

Extensions of the method for other real option valuations have been developed such as contract guarantee (put option), [[Datar–Mathews method for real option valuation#Multi-stage (Compound) option|Multi-stage]], Early Launch (American option), and others.

== Implementation ==

The DM Method may be implemented using [[Monte-Carlo simulation]],<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brigatti |first1=E |author2=Macias F. |author3=Souza M.O. |author4=Zubelli J.P. |editor1-last=Aid |editor1-first=R |title=A Hedged Monte Carlo Approach to Real Option Pricing |date=2015 |publisher=Springer |location=New York, NY |isbn=978-1-4939-2733-3 |page=7 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4939-2733-3_10 |arxiv=1509.03577 }}</ref> or in a simplified algebraic or other form (see the Range Option below).

Using simulation, for each sample, the engine draws a random variable from both <math>\tilde S_T \text { and } \tilde X_T,</math> calculates their present values, and takes the difference.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=Z9xGYj7_uFgC&q=Tutorials+in+Operations+Research+2007 Business Engineering: A Practical Approach to Valuing High-Risk, High-Return Projects Using Real Options] Tutorials in Operations Research 2007, Operations Research Tools and Applications: Glimpses of Future Technologies, p157–175</ref><ref>[http://www.vwl.uni-freiburg.de/fakultaet/wt/data/downloads/general/1%20Agliardi%20-%20Mathews%20and%20Salmon.pdf Business Engineering: A Practical Approach to Valuing High-Risk, High-Return Projects Using Real Options] [[INFORMS]] Annual Meeting, November 4–7, 2007</ref> Fig. 2A. The difference value is compared to zero, the maximum of the two is determined, and the resulting value recorded by the simulation engine. Here, reflecting the optionality inherent in the project, a forecast of a net negative value outcome corresponds to an abandoned project, and has a zero value. Fig. 2B. The resulting values create a payoff distribution representing the economically rational set of plausible, discounted value forecasts of the project at time ''T<sub>0</sub>''.

{{multiple image
 | align = center
 | direction = horizontal
 | total_width = 690
 | image1 = Datar_Mathews_Real_Option_Method_Wikipedia_Fig_2A_Net_Profit_Present_Value_Distribution.jpg
 | caption1 = Fig. 2A Net profit present-value distribution
 | image2 = Datar_Mathews_Real_Option_Method_Wikipedia_Fig_2B_Rational_Decision_Distribution.jpg
 | caption2 = Fig. 2B Rational decision distribution
 | image3 = Datar_Mathews_Real_Option_Method_Wikipedia_Fig_2C_Payoff_Distribution_and_Option_Value.jpg
 | caption3 = Fig. 2C Payoff distribution and option value
}}

When sufficient payoff values have been recorded, typically a few hundred, then the mean, or expected value, of the payoff distribution is calculated. Fig. 2C. The option value is the expected value, the first moment of all positive NPVs and zeros, of the payoff distribution.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Kozlova |first=Mariia |date= April 2015 |title=Analyzing the Effects of the New Renewable Energy Policy in Russia on Investments into Wind, Solar and Small Hydro Power |type=Thesis |pages=62–66 |publisher= Lappeenranta University of Technology}}</ref>

A simple interpretation is:

: <math>\text{Real option value} = \text{average} \left[\max\left(\text{operating profit}-\text{launch costs}\right),0)\right]</math>

where ''operating profit'' and ''launch costs'' are the appropriately discounted range of cash flows to time ''T<sub>0</sub>''.<ref>{{cite book | doi=10.1109/CIFER.2009.4937494 | title=2009 IEEE Symposium on Computational Intelligence for Financial Engineering | date=March 2009 | last1=Mathews | first1=Scott H. | chapter=Tutorial CIFER-T2 Boeing's method for valuing high-risk high-return technology projects using real options | pages=x | isbn=978-1-4244-2774-1 }}</ref>

The DM Option can also be interpreted as a logical function. Frequently the simulation is provided by a [[Monte Carlo method|Monte Carlo function]] embedded in a spreadsheet, such as [[Microsoft Excel]]. The Excel logic function for a DM [[call option]] is:

: <math>\text{Call option value} = \overline { \text {IF}((\tilde S_0 > \tilde X_0),(\tilde S_0 - \tilde X_0),0)} </math> , where the overline represents an average value function.

The Excel logic function for a DM [[put option]] is:

: <math>\text{Put option value} = \overline { \text{IF}((\tilde S_0 < \tilde X_0),(-\tilde S_0 + \tilde X_0),0)} </math>

It is interesting to note that for any operating profit distribution with the same launch cost (strike price) can result in both a call option value as well as a put option value. Changing the call and put options to two different strike prices results in a [[collar (finance)|collar]] strategy.

Without the averaging function, the option value can also be understood as a distribution (<math>\tilde C_0</math>) reflecting the uncertainty of the underlying variables.

== DM Option Variations ==

=== Algebraic lognormal form ===

The DM real option can be considered a generalized form for option valuation. Its simulation produces a truncated present value distribution of which the mean value is interpreted to be the option value. With certain boundary conditions, the DM option can be reformulated algebraically as a conditional expectation of a lognormal distribution similar to the form and characteristics of a typical financial option, such as the European, single stage Black-Scholes financial option. This section illustrates the transformation of the DM real option to its algebraic lognormal form and its relationship to the Black-Scholes financial option formula. The process illuminates some of the more technical elements of the option formulation thereby providing further insight to the underlying concepts.

[[File:Fig. 4 Concept of conditional probability distribution and mean of tail.png|thumb|left|256x256px|'''Fig. 3 Concept of conditional probability distribution and mean of tail''']]

The lognormal form of the DM Method remains a simple concept based on the same computation procedures as the simulation form. It is the [[conditional expectation]] of the discounted projected [[future value]] outcome distribution, <math>\tilde S_T</math>, less a predetermined purchase cost (strike price or launch cost), <math>\bar X_T</math>, (modeled in this example as a scalar value) multiplied by the probability of that truncated distribution greater than a threshold—nominally 0. A conditional expectation is the expected value of the [[truncated distribution]] (mean of the tail), ''MT'', computed with respect to its [[conditional probability distribution]]<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Gyoshev |first1=Stanley B. |last2=Gombola |first2=Michael |title=A Separating Equilibrium for Stock Repurchase Programs via PUT Options: Transforming a Mathematical Proof into Visual Form |date=2012-12-04 |pages=4, 17 |ssrn=2185093}}</ref> (Fig. 3).
[[File:Fig. 5 Time differentiated discounting appears to shift X relative to S.png|thumb|300x256px|'''Fig. 4 Time differentiated discounting appears to shift ''X'' relative to ''S''''']]

The option calculation procedure values the project investment (option purchase), ''C<sub>0</sub>'', at ''T<sub>0</sub>''. For the DM option the time differentiated discounting (''R'' and ''r'') results in an apparent shift of the projected value outcome distribution, <math>\tilde S</math>, relative to the <math>\tilde X</math>, or the scalar mean <math>\bar X</math> in the example shown in Fig. 4.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.investmentscience.com/Content/newsArticles/news3.html|title=The Two-Rate Method of Discounting|last=Luenberger|first=David|date=Autumn 1998|website=Investment Science Newsletter|publisher=Department of Management Science & Engineering, Stanford University|access-date=2019-11-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | doi=10.2514/6.2011-6839 | title=11th AIAA Aviation Technology, Integration, and Operations (ATIO) Conference | chapter=Option-Based Approach to Value Engine Maintenance Cost Guarantees and Engine Maintenance Contracts | series=Aviation Technology, Integration, and Operations (ATIO) Conferences | date=20 September 2011 | publisher=American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics | last1=Justin | first1=Cedric | last2=Mavris | first2=Dimitri | isbn=978-1-60086-941-9 }}</ref> This relative shift sets up the conditional expectation of the truncated distribution at ''T<sub>0</sub>''.

In a lognormal distribution for a project future value outcome, <math>\tilde S_T</math>, both the mean, <math>\bar S_T</math>, and standard deviation, <math>SD_T</math>, must be specified.<ref name="auto">{{Cite book |chapter=Valuing High-Risk High-Return technology Projects Using Real Options |title=The Handbook of Technology Management: Core Concepts, Financial Tools and Techniques, Operations and Innovation Management |last=Mathews |first=Scott |publisher=Wiley |year=2010 |isbn=978-0470249475 |editor-last=Bidgoli |editor-first=Hossein |volume=1 |location=Hoboken, NJ |pages=581–600}}</ref> The standard deviation, <math>SD_T</math>, of the distribution <math>\tilde S_T</math> is proportionately discounted along with the distribution, <math>SD_0 = SD_Te^{-RT}.</math><ref>Hereafter, variables are assumed to be scaler unless otherwise specified as a distribution indicated by a tilde <math>\sim.</math></ref>

The parameters of <math> \sigma \text{ and } \mu </math>, of a [[Log-normal distribution#Generation and parameters|lognormal]] at ''T<sub>0</sub>'' can be derived from the values <math>SD_0 \text{ and } S_0 </math> respectively, as:

:<math> \sigma= \sqrt {\ln\left[1+\left(\tfrac{SD}{S}\right)^2\right] } \text { where } \tfrac {SD}{S}=\tfrac {SD_0}{S_0}= \tfrac {SD_T}{S_T}</math>
:<math>\mu = \ln \left( \tfrac {S_0}{\sqrt {1 + \left( \tfrac {SD}{S} \right) ^2 }} \right)=\ln S_0 -0.5 \ln \left[ 1 + \left( \tfrac {SD}{S} \right) ^2 \right]=\ln S_0-0.5 \sigma^2.</math>

The [[Log-normal distribution#Conditional expectation|conditional expectation]] of the discounted value outcome is the mean of the tail ''MT'':
:<math>E \left[ \tilde S \mid \tilde S \geq X \right]=S_0\left[\tfrac{N\left(\tfrac{\mu+\sigma^2-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}{N\left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}\right]\text{ where }N(\cdot)</math> is the [[cumulative distribution function]] of the [[standard normal distribution]] (N(0,1)).
The probability of the project being in the money and launched (“exercised”) is <math>N\left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right).</math>

The project investment (option) value is:
:<math>C_0=\left\{S_0\left[\tfrac{ N\left(\tfrac{\sigma^2+\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}{N\left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}\right]-X_0\right\} N \left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right).</math>

The involved lognormal mathematics can be burdensome and opaque for some business practices within a corporation. However, several simplifications can ease that burden and provide clarity without sacrificing the soundness of the option calculation. One simplification is the employment of the [[standard normal distribution]], also known as the Z-distribution, which has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. It is common practice to convert a normal distribution to a standard normal and then use the [[standard normal table]] to find the value of probabilities.

Define as the [[Standard normal table#Conversion|standard normal variable]]: <math>Z=\tfrac{\left(\ln X_0-\mu\right)}{\sigma}.</math>

The conditional expectation of the discounted value outcome is:
:<math>S_0\left[\tfrac{N\left(\tfrac{\mu+\sigma^2-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}{N\left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)}\right]=S_0\left[\tfrac{ N\left(\sigma-Z\right)}{ N\left(-Z\right)}\right].</math>

Then probability of the project being in the money and launched (“exercised”) is: <math> N\left(\tfrac{\mu-\ln X_0}{\sigma}\right)=N\left(-Z\right).</math>

The Datar-Mathews lognormal option value simplifies to:
:<math>C_\text{DM}=\left \{S_0\left[\tfrac{ N\left(\sigma-Z\right)}{ N\left(-Z\right)}\right]-X_0\right\} N\left(-Z\right)=S_0 N\left(\sigma-Z\right)-X_0 N\left(-Z\right).</math>

==== Transformation to the Black-Scholes Option ====

The [[Black–Scholes#Black–Scholes formula|Black–Scholes option formula]] (as well as the [[Binomial options pricing model|binomial lattice]]) is a special case of the simulated DM real option. With subtle, but notable differences, the logarithmic form of the DM Option can be algebraically transformed into The Black-Scholes option formula.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Collan |first1=Mikael |title=Thoughts about Selected Models for the Valuation of Real Options |journal=Acta Universitatis Palackianae Olomucensis. Facultas Rerum Naturalium. Mathematica |date=2011 |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=5–12 |url=http://dml.cz/dmlcz/141747 |issn=0231-9721}}</ref> The real option valuation is based on an approximation of the future value outcome distribution, which may be lognormal, at time ''T<sub>T</sub>'' projected (discounted) to ''T<sub>0</sub>''. In contrast, the [[Black-Scholes]] is based on a lognormal distribution projected from historical asset returns to present time ''T<sub>0</sub>''.<ref>The Black-Scholes model classically assumed that a lognormal distribution most closely approximated the statistical distribution of an asset’s returns. This assumption conveniently simplified the mathematics of the option pricing formula and it remains a useful approximation. [[Black–Scholes model#Black-Scholes in practice|In reality security prices do not follow a strict stationary log-normal process.]] The value results using the Black–Scholes model differ slightly from real world financial option prices in part because of simplifying assumptions of the model.</ref> Analysis of these historical trends results in a calculation termed the [[volatility (finance)]] factor. For Black-Scholes (BS) the [[Black–Scholes model#Notation|volatility]] factor is <math>\sigma_{BS}\sqrt  T</math>.<ref>Variance of a lognormal distribution is <math>\sigma ^2 </math>, and its standard deviation is <math>\sigma</math>. Variance of stock prices are assumed to follow a [[Wiener process|Wiener Process]] or [[geometric Brownian motion]] proportional to time <math>\sigma ^2 T</math> and its standard deviation (or volatility) is <math>\sigma \sqrt  T</math>. The relationship of Black Scholes (BS) volatility (annualized) and the logarithmic standard deviation is then: <math>\sigma _{BS} \sqrt T =\sigma  . </math> Alternatively, <math>\sigma _{BS} =\sqrt \tfrac { \ln \left [ 1+ \left ( \tfrac {SD} {S} \right ) ^2 \right ]} {T} </math> where ''S'' is the mean and ''SD'' is the standard deviation of the present value lognormal distribution.</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Houstecky |first1=Petr |title=Why Is Volatility Proportional to the Square Root of Time? |url=https://www.macroption.com/why-is-volatility-proportional-to-square-root-of-time/ |website=Macroptioni}}</ref>

The following lognormal distribution with a standard deviation <math>\sigma</math> is replaced by the volatility factor <math>\sigma_{BS}\sqrt  T</math>.

:<math>\left( \sigma -Z \right)=\sigma -\tfrac{\left(\ln X_0-\mu \right)}{\sigma}=\ln S_0 -0.5 \ln \left[ 1 + \left( \tfrac {SD}{S} \right) ^2 \right]=\tfrac{\left[ \ln\left( \tfrac{S_0}{X_T}\right)+\left( r+\tfrac{\sigma^2_\text {BS}}{2}\right) T\right]}{\left(\sigma_\text {BS} \sqrt T\right)}=d_1 \text { where } \ln X_T = \ln X_0 -rT </math>

:<math>\left(-Z \right)= -\tfrac{\left(\ln X_0-\mu \right)}{\sigma}=\tfrac { \left [ \left (\ln S_0 -0.5 \sigma ^2 \right )-\ln X_0\right]}{\sigma}=\tfrac{\left[ \ln\left( \tfrac{S_0}{X_T}\right)+\left( r-\tfrac{\sigma^2_\text {BS}}{2}\right) T\right]}{\left(\sigma_\text {BS} \sqrt T\right)}=d_1-\sigma_\text {BS} \sqrt T=d_2</math>

The Black-Scholes option value simplifies to its familiar form:
:<math>C_\text{BS}=S N\left( d_1\right)-X_Te^{-rT} N\left( d_2\right)</math>

[[File:Fig 3 Comparison of Black Scholes and Datar-Mathews frameworks.png|thumb|550x550px|Fig 5. Left: Comparison of Black Scholes and Datar-Mathews frameworks. Right: Detail of tail of distribution at T<sub>0</sub>.]]

The terms ''N''(''d<sub>1</sub>'') and ''N''(''d<sub>2</sub>'') are applied [[Black–Scholes#Black–Scholes formula|in the calculation of the Black–Scholes formula]], and are expressions related to operations on lognormal distributions;<ref name="Chance 99-02">Don Chance (2011). [http://www.bus.lsu.edu/academics/finance/faculty/dchance/Instructional/TN99-02.pdf ''Derivation and Interpretation of the Black–Scholes Model''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110911010851/http://www.bus.lsu.edu/academics/finance/faculty/dchance/Instructional/TN99-02.pdf |date=2011-09-11 }}.</ref> see section [[Black–Scholes#Interpretation|"Interpretation"]] under [[Black–Scholes]]. Referring to Fig. 5 and using the lognormal form of the DM Option, it is possible to derive certain insights to the internal operation of an option:

:<math>N\left(\sigma-Z\right)=N\left( d_1\right)</math>
:<math>N\left(-Z\right)=N\left( d_2\right)</math>

''N''(''-Z'') or ''N''(''d<sub>2</sub>'') is a measure of the area of the [[Probability distribution#Basic terms|tail of the distribution]], ''MT'' (delineated by ''X<sub>0</sub>''), relative to that of the entire distribution, e.g. the probability of tail of the distribution, at time ''T<sub>0</sub>''. Fig. 5, Right. The true probability of expiring in-the-money in the real (“physical”) world is calculated at time ''T<sub>0</sub>'', the launch or strike date, measured by area of the tail of the distribution. ''N''(''σ-Z'') or ''N''(''d<sub>1</sub>'') is the value of the option payoff relative to that of the asset. <math>N(d_1) = \left[MT \ x\ N(d_2)\right]/S_0,</math>  where ''MT'' is the mean of the tail at time ''T<sub>0</sub>''.

=== Data patterns === <!-- DM Option – Simplify Using Data Patterns -->
A simplified DM Method computation conforms to the same essential features—it is the discounted [[conditional expectation]] of the discounted projected future value outcome distribution, or <math>MT</math>, less a discounted cost, <math> X_0</math>, multiplied by the probability of exercise, <math>N\left(-Z\right).</math> The value of the DM Method option can be understood as <math>C_0=\left(MT - X_0\right)\ x\ N\left(-Z\right).</math> This simplified formulation has strong parallels to an [[expected value]] calculation.

Businesses that collect historical data may be able to leverage the similarity of assumptions across related projects facilitating the calculation of option values. One resulting simplification is the ''Uncertainty Ratio'', <math>\textstyle UR=(SD/S)</math>, which can often be modeled as a constant for similar projects. ''UR'' is the degree of certainty by which the projected future cash flows can be estimated. ''UR'' is invariant of time <math>\textstyle\left(\tfrac{SD_T}{S_T}=\tfrac{SD_0}{S_0}\right)</math> with values typically between 0.35 and 1.0 for many multi-year business projects.

Applying this observation as a constant, ''K'', to the above formulas results in a simpler formulation:
:<math>\text {Define }K=\sigma =\sqrt \left [\ln (1+UR^2) \right ]\text {, and }\mu = \ln S_0-0.5\sigma ^2=\ln S_0-0.5K^2.</math>

:<math>Z=\frac {(\ln X_0-\mu)}{\sigma}=\tfrac {\ln \left (\tfrac {X_0}{S_0}\right )}{K}+0.5K\text {, and } -Z=\tfrac {\ln \left (\tfrac {S_0}{X_0}\right )}{K}-0.5K.</math>

<math>Z</math> is normally distributed and the values can be accessed in a table of [[Standard normal table#Conversion|standard normal variables]]. The resulting real option value can be derived simply on a hand-held calculator once K is determined:
:<math>C_0=S_0 N\left (\sigma-Z\right )-X_0 N\left (-Z\right )= S_0 N\left (K-Z\right )-X_0 N\left (-Z\right ).</math>

=== Triangular form (Range Option) ===

Given the difficulty in estimating the lognormal distribution mean and standard deviation of future returns, other distributions instead are more often applied for real options used in business decision making. The [[Sampling (statistics)|sampled]] [[Probability distribution|distributions]] may take any form, although the [[triangular distribution]] is often used, [[Triangular distribution#Business simulations|as is typical for low data situations]], followed by a [[uniform distribution (continuous)]] or a [[beta distribution]].<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Alabi |first=Olabode |date=2010-04-30|title=Evaluation Method for Strategic Investments |type=Dissertation |publisher= University of Nebraska - Lincoln |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/imsediss }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Peters |first1=Linda |s2cid=56465582 |title=Impact of Probability Distributions on Real Options Valuation |journal=Journal of Infrastructure Systems |date=September 2016 |volume=22 |issue=3 |article-number=04016005 |doi=10.1061/(ASCE)IS.1943-555X.0000289|hdl=10067/1319100151162165141 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> This approach is useful for early-stage estimates of project option value when there has not been sufficient time or resources to gather the necessary quantitative information required for a complete cash flow simulation, or in a portfolio of projects when simulation of all the projects is too computationally demanding.<ref>[http://www.iriweb.org/Public_Site/RTM/Volume_54_Year_2011/September-October2011/Innovation_Portfolio_Architecture_-_Part2.aspx Innovation Portfolio Architecture – Part 2: Attribute Selection and Valuation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140830095223/http://www.iriweb.org/Public_Site/RTM/Volume_54_Year_2011/September-October2011/Innovation_Portfolio_Architecture_-_Part2.aspx|date=2014-08-30}}. [[Research-Technology Management]] Vol. 54, No. 5 September–October 2011</ref> Regardless of the distribution chosen, the procedure remains the same for a real option valuation. 
[[File:Fig. 7 Triangular conditional probability distribution.png|thumb|left|'''Fig. 6 Triangular conditional probability distribution''']]

{| class="wikitable floatright" | width="425"
|- 
|'''Innovation Project Quick Contingent Value Estimate'''
|-
|
With most likely PV operating cash flow of $8.5M, but a 3-year capital cost of roughly $20M, the NPV of the important innovation project was deeply negative and the manager is considering abandoning it. Corporate sales analytics estimated with 95% certainty (double-sided 1-in-10 chance) the revenues could be as low as $4M or as high as $34M. (Fig. 7) Because of the large potential upside, the manager believes a small initial investment might resolve the project's downside uncertainties and reveal its potential value.<ref>{{cite SSRN |last1=Sadowsky |first1=Jeffery R. |title=The Value of Learning in the Product Development Stage: A Real Options Approach  |date=May 10, 2005 |page=9 |ssrn=721597 }}</ref> [[File:Range Option showing triangular distribution V2.png|alt=|thumb|250x250px|'''Fig. 7 DM Range Option with triangular distribution. (Background: comparable lognormal distribution.)''']]

Using the DM Range Option as a guide, the manager calculated the expected contingent value of the project upside to be about $25M [≈ (2*$20M + $34M)/3]. Furthermore, there is a probability of one-in-four {25% ≈ ($34M - $20M)<sup>2</sup> /[ ($34M - $4M)($34M-$8.5M)]} that the project revenues will be greater than $20M. With these calculations, the manager estimates the innovation project option value is $1.25M [= ($25M-$20M) * 25%]. Using this value, the manager justifies this initial investment (about 6% of the capital cost) into the project, sufficient to resolve some of the key uncertainties. The project can always be abandoned should the intermediate development results not measure up, but the investment losses will be minimized. (Later using corporate historical data patterns, an analyst converted the values from a three-point estimate to a DM Option calculation, and demonstrated that the result would differ by less than 10%.)
|}

For a triangular distribution, sometimes referred to as [[three-point estimation]], the mode value corresponds to the “most-likely” scenario, and the other two other scenarios, “pessimistic” and “optimistic”, represent plausible deviations from the most-likely scenario (often modeled as approximating a two-sided 1-out-of-10 likelihood or 95% confidence).<ref name="auto"/><ref>{{cite thesis|last=Onkham|first=Wilawan|date=2013|title=A Real Option Dynamic Decision Framework for Operational Innovations|type=PhD|page=44|publisher=University of Central Florida|url=https://stars.library.ucf.edu/etd/2873|degree=Doctoral}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Naedele |first1=Martin |last2=Chen |first2=Hong-Mei |last3=Kazman |first3=Rick |last4=Cai |first4=Yuanfang |last5=Xiao |first5=Lu |last6=Silva |first6=Carlos V.A. |title=Manufacturing execution systems: A vision for managing software development |journal=Journal of Systems and Software |date=March 2015 |volume=101 |pages=59–68 |doi=10.1016/j.jss.2014.11.015}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |last=Patregnani |first=Giulia |date=2014-10-13 |title=The Value of Synergies through the Real Options Lenses |type=Graduate Theses, MS in Finance and Strategic Management |pages=63–65 |publisher=Copenhagen School of Business  |hdl=10417/4840 }}</ref> This range of estimates results in the eponymous name for the option, the DM Range Option.<ref>{{Cite journal |jstor=43240438 |title=Valuing Risky Projects with Real Options |volume=52 |issue=5 |date=September–October 2009 |journal=Research Technology Management |last=Mathews |first=Scott |pages=32–41 |language=en|doi=10.1080/08956308.2009.11657587 }}</ref> The DM Range Option method is similar to the [[Fuzzy pay-off method for real option valuation|fuzzy method for real options]]. The following example (Fig. 6) uses a range of future estimated operating profits of ''a'' (pessimistic), ''b'' (optimistic) and ''m'' (mode or most-likely).

For <math>T_0</math> discount ''a'', ''b'' and ''m'' by <math>e^{-RT}\text { and } X_0=X_T e^{-rT}.</math>

The classic DM Method presumes that the strike price is represented by a random variable (distribution <math>\tilde X_0</math>) with the option solution derived by [[Monte Carlo methods in finance#Applicability|simulation]]. Alternatively, without the burden of performing a simulation, applying the average or mean scalar value of the launch cost distribution <math>\bar X_0</math> (strike price) results in a conservative estimate of DM Range Option value. If the launch cost is predetermined as a scalar value, then the DM Range Option value calculation is exact.

The expected value of the truncated triangular distribution (mean of the right tail), is <math>MT=\tfrac {\left (2X_0+b \right)}{3}.</math>

The probability of the project being in the money and launched is the proportional area of the truncated distribution relative to the complete triangular distribution. (See Fig. 16) This partial expectation is computed by the [[cumulative distribution function]] (CDF) given the probability distribution will be found at a value greater than or equal to ''X'':

:<math>P(X_0|X_0\ge x)=\frac{\left ( b-X_0 \right)^2}{\left [ \left ( b-a \right)\left(b-m\right ) \right ]}.</math>

The DM Range Option value, or project investment, is:

:<math> C_0 = \left (MT - X_0 \right )\cdot P\left (X_0 \vert X_0 \ge x \right) =\left ( MT - X_0 \right )\cdot \left \{ \frac{\left ( b-X_0 \right)^2}{\left [ \left ( b-a \right)\left(b-m\right ) \right ]} \right \}. </math>

:<math>\text {Note: }\mu =0.5*\ln (a+b)\text {, }\sigma=0.25*\ln (b/a)\text {, and } UR= \sqrt {e^ {\sigma^2} -1}.</math><ref>applies [[Log-normal distribution#Geometric of multiplicative methods|geometric mean]]</ref>

Use of a DM Range Option facilitates the application of real option valuation to future project investments. The DM Range Option provides an estimate of valuation that differs marginally with that of the DM Option algebraic lognormal distribution form. However, the projected future value outcome, ''S'', of a project is rarely based on a lognormal distribution derived from historical asset returns, as is a financial option. Rather, the future value outcome, ''S'', (as well as the strike price, ''X'', and the standard deviation, ''SD''), is more than likely a three-point estimation based on engineering and marketing parameters. Therefore, the ease of application of the DM Range Option is often justified by its [[Monte Carlo methods in finance#Level of complexity|expediency]] and is sufficient to estimate the conditional value of a future project.

== Multi-stage (Compound) Option ==
Timothy Luehrman in an [[Harvard Business Review|HBR]] article states: “In financial terms, a business strategy is much more like a series of options than a series of static cash flows or even [[decision tree model|decision trees]]. Executing a strategy almost always involves making a sequence of risky decisions.”<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Luehrman |first=Timothy |date= September–October 1998 |title= Strategy as a Portfolio of Real Options |journal= Harvard Business Review |volume=76 |issue=5 |pages=87–99 |pmid=10185434 }}</ref> A multi-stage business strategy valuation can be modeled as a sequence of staged contingent investment decisions structured as a series of DM single-stage options. [[File:Three-stage option value distribution.jpg|thumb|right|'''Fig. 8 Three-stage option value distribution.''']]

In valuing a complex strategic opportunity, a multi-stage, or [[compound option]],<ref>Can also be 'multi-period' or 'multinomial' option</ref> is a more accurate, but more mathematically demanding, approach than simpler calculations using [[decision tree model]], [[Influence diagrams approach|influence diagrams]], or [[Lattice model (finance)|lattice]]/[[Binomial options pricing model|binomial]] model approaches.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter = Multistage real options |title= The Economics of Human Systems Integration |last=Pennock |first=Michael  |publisher=Wiley |year=2010 |doi=10.1002/9780470642627.ch10  |pages=185–208|isbn= 978-0-470-48676-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1= De Reyck |first1= Bert |last2= Degraeve |first2= Zeger |last3= Vandenborre |first3= Roger |year= 2008 |title= Project options valuation with net present value and decision tree analysis |journal= European Journal of Operational Research |volume=184 |issue=1 |pages=341–355|doi= 10.1016/j.ejor.2006.07.047 |url= https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/lkcsb_research/6752 }}</ref> Each stage is contingent on the execution or abandonment (gain/success or loss/failure) of the subsequent stage accounting for the investment cost of the preceding stages.
The literature references several approaches to modeling a multi-stage option.<ref>U.S. Patent No. 7,676,412 (issued March 9, 2010). Path dependent multistage option</ref><ref>U.S. Patent No. 7,676,413 (issued March 9, 2010). Emergent multistage option, bin method</ref><ref>U.S. Patent No. 7,698,189 (issued April 13, 2010). Emergent multistage option, zero cross method</ref><ref>U.S. Patent No. 7,747,503 (issued June 29, 2010). Contingent exercise multistage option</ref><ref>U.S. Patent No. 7,747,504 (issued June 29, 2010). Emergent multistage option, arc method</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herath |first1=H. S. |last2=Park |first2=C. S. |year= 2002 |title= Multi-stage capital investment opportunities as compound real options |journal= The Engineering Economist |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1080/00137910208965021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Koussis |first1=N. |last2=Martzoukos |first2=S. H. |last3=Trigeorgis |first3=L.|year= 2013 |title= Multi-stage product development with exploration, value-enhancing, preemptive and innovation options |journal= Journal of Banking & Finance |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=174–190 |doi=10.1016/j.jbankfin.2012.08.020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Alexander |first1=Carol |last2=Chen |first2=Xi |last3=Ward |first3=Charles |year= 2021 |title= Risk-adjusted valuation for real option decisions |journal= Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization |volume=191 |pages=1046–1064|doi=10.1016/j.jebo.2021.09.011 |arxiv=2109.04793 |url=http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/101747/1/Risk-Adjusted_Valuation_for_Real_Option_Decisions.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Haug |first1=Espen Gaarder |title=The Complete Guide to Option Pricing Formulas |date=January 2007 |publisher=McGraw-Hill Education |isbn=978-0071389976 |pages=132–135 |edition=2nd}}</ref><ref>Geske in 1977 offers a classic model for pricing financial options on options. (See Espen Gaarder Haug reference.) It assumes a single termination date for a contract of two periods. The DM multi-stage option applies to real options (i.e. no contract, only valuation) and assumes multiple possible terminations dependent on the state of development.</ref> A three-stage option (1 [[Proof of concept]], 2 Prototype Development, 3 Launch/ Production) can be modeled as:<ref>The model is premised on a [[stochastic simulation]] to generate the cash flows with initial values of <math> \tilde S_0 \text { and }\tilde X_i </math> and projected with a [[forward rate]] and volatility.</ref>
<math> \begin{alignat}{2}C_0 = E \Bigl(&  if \langle \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} \geq \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \right ), if \lbrace \left ( \tilde {S}_2e^{-Rt_0} \geq \tilde {X}_2e^{-rt_0} + \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \right ), \\
&\left [ max \left (\tilde {S}_3e^{-Rt_0} - \tilde {X}_3e^{-rt_0},0 \right ) - \tilde {X}_2e^{-rt_0} - \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0}\right ], - \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \rbrace ,0 \rangle \Bigr).\end{alignat}</math>

The valuation then occurs in reverse order conditioned on success or failure at each stage. The nominal value of this three-stage option is the mean of the multiple (typically several thousand k trials) simulated cash flows.
[[File:Path dependency for selection of P* candidates.jpg|thumb|right|'''Fig. 9 Path dependency for selection of P* candidates.''']]

While the valuation of a multi-stage option is of technical interest, the principal focus of a project manager is the maximization of the probability of success and overall project value. The astute selection of project stage [[Milestone (project management)|milestones]] can simultaneously achieve these goals while also providing project management clarity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1= Bhattacharya |first1=S. |last2=Gaba |first2=V. |last3=Hasija |first3=S. |year= 2015 |title= A comparison of milestone-based and buyout options contracts for coordinating R&D partnerships |journal= Management Science |volume=61 |issue=5 |pages=963–978|doi=10.1287/mnsc.2013.1874 |url=https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/lkcsb_research/5104 }}</ref><ref>Setting project milestones, at least for the first, and possibly the second build stage, is key to managing these ‘make or break’ investment decisions, without engaging senior management in the mathematics of valuing multi-stage options.</ref>  Milestone set points are determined by specifying the option payoff for the end stage ''n'' value distribution, and [[backcasting]]. Prospective milestones, or value thresholds, for each stage ''i'' are designated <math>P_i^*</math> (pronounced ‘P-star’). Multiple simulated cash flows, projected from <math> \tilde {S}_0 </math>, create a pattern of option value responses for each stage revealing prospective candidate milestones.<ref>For example, the perspective from stage <math> i-1 </math>, with an execution cost of <math> -\tilde {X}_{i-1}e^{-rt_0},</math> is a value range from a maximum of <math> \left (\tilde {S}_ie^{-Rt_0} -  \tilde {X}_ie^{-rt_0},0\right ) - \tilde {X}_{i-1}e^{-rt_0} </math> to a minimum of <math> - \tilde {X}_{i-1}e^{-rt_0} </math>.</ref> The simulation evaluates the payoff option values <math>E \lbrace \left [ max \left ( \tilde {S}_ie^{-Rt_0} - \tilde {X}_ie^{-rt_0},0 \right ) - \tilde {X}_{i-1}e^{-rt_0}\right ] \geq P_i^*\rbrace. </math><ref>Given prospect at stage <math>n-1,</math> and incurring cost <math>-\tilde {X}_{n-1}e^{-rt_0},</math> what is the milestone hurdle or threshold <math>P_i^*</math> value that will maximize <math> \left [ max \left ( \tilde {S}_ie^{-Rt_0} - \tilde {X}_ie^{-rt_0},0\right ) - \tilde {X}_{i-1}e^{-rt_0}\right ]? </math></ref> A simulation of thousands of trials results in a valuation and ranking of a large sets of data pairs for each stage i: stage ''i'' option values mapped to candidate <math>P_i^*</math> values.
[[File:Range of prospective milestones.jpg|thumb|left|'''Fig. 10 Range of prospective milestones; optimal P** at vertex.''']]
A [[parabola|parabolic]] distribution of data point pairs graphs the sorted range of stage ''i'' option values against prospective <math>P_i^*</math> milestone values. If selected <math>P_i^*</math> threshold is set too low, there are excessive failures to exercise, <math>\left ( \tilde {S}_ie^{-Rt_0} < P_i^*\right )</math>, and numerically the expected option value is reduced. Alternatively, if selected <math>P_i^*</math> threshold is set too high, then there are insufficient instances of successful exercises, and numerically the expected option value is reduced again. The optimal milestone <math>P_i^{**}</math> (‘P-double star’) value that emerges during simulation maximizes the overall project option value by balancing gains and losses.
[[File:Emergent option value determined with P** candidates.jpg|thumb|right|'''Fig. 11 Emergent option value determined with P** candidates.''']]
A three-stage option optimized for management by milestone and value maximization can be modeled as:<ref>The value of this optimized option is almost always (significantly) greater and not equivalent to the nominal value of the three-stage option above.</ref>

<math> \begin{alignat}{2}C_0=E \Bigl(&  if \langle \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_1^{**} \right ), if \lbrace \left ( \tilde {S}_2e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_2^{**} \right ), \\
&\left [ max \left (\tilde {S}_3e^{-Rt_0} - \tilde {X}_3e^{-rt_0},0 \right ) - \tilde {X}_2e^{-rt_0} - \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0}\right ], - \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \rbrace ,0 \rangle \Bigr). \end{alignat}</math><ref>Alternative milestone values can be set as <math> \tilde {S}_ie^{Rt_i} \geq P_i^{**}</math>based on future projected values. Once adjusted the value of <math>C_0</math> is unchanged.</ref>

Or, succinctly,

<math> C_0=E\left [max \left (\tilde {S}_ne^{-Rt_0} - \tilde {X}_ne^{-rt_0},0\right ) - \tilde {X}_{n-i}e^{-rt_0}\right ] \times \mathbb{P}\left ( \tilde {S}_1^{n-1}e^{-Rt_0}\geq P_1^{n-1 **}\right ). </math><ref>A multi-stage option can be valued with fractional parts. Below is an example for a three-stage option: 
<math> \begin{alignat}{7}
&	1. \quad \mathbb{P}  \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} < P_1^{**}\right ) \times 0 \\

&	2. \quad \mathbb{P}  \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_1^{**} \; \And \; \tilde {S}_2e^{-Rt_0} < P_2^{**} \right ) \times - \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \\

&	3. \quad \mathbb{P}  \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_1^{**} \; \And \; \tilde {S}_2e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_2^{**} \; \And \; \tilde {S}_3e^{-Rt_0} < \tilde {X}_3e^{-rt_0} \right ) \\
&   \qquad  \;            \times - \left ( \tilde {X}_2e^{-rt_0} + \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \right ) \\

&	4. \quad \mathbb{P}  \left ( \tilde {S}_1e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_1^{**} \; \And \; \tilde {S}_2e^{-Rt_0} \geq P_2^{**} \; \And \; \tilde {S}_3e^{-Rt_0} \geq \tilde {X}_3e^{-rt_0} \right ) \\
&    \qquad  \;           \times \left [ \tilde {S}_3e^{-Rt_0} - \left ( \tilde {X}_3e^{-rt_0} + \tilde {X}_2e^{-rt_0} + \tilde {X}_1e^{-rt_0} \right ) \right ] \\

&	5. \quad \sum \left (1:4 \right ) \\
\end{alignat} </math></ref>

Note that typically <math>P_i^{**}\gg \tilde {X}_ie^{-rt_0}.</math> The insertion of these carefully determined conditional milestones increases the overall value of the nominal multi-stage option because each successive stage has been optimized to maximize the option value. By use of selected milestones, the project manager achieves the goals of increasing the probability of success and overall project value while also reducing the project managerial burden.

== Governance and real options ==
Real options identify and value managerial flexibility, while [[project governance|governance]] determines how that flexibility is incorporated into investment decisions. Conventional projects evaluated using NPV also require governance, including opportunity evaluation, resource allocation, project reviews, and performance controls.<ref>https://www.pmi.org/pmbok-guide-standards/practice-guides/governance</ref> Real-options (RO) analysis, however, is particularly applicable to opportunities characterized by substantial uncertainty and managerial flexibility. In such cases, an organization can limit its initial commitment while retaining the ability to invest further, modify the project, defer investment, or abandon the opportunity as additional information becomes available.<ref name="trott26">{{cite book|title=Innovation Management and New Product Development|last=Trott|first=Paul|publisher=Prentice Hall|year=2005|isbn=0-273-68643-7}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huchzermeier |first1=Arnd |last2=Loch |first2=Christoph H. |year=2001 |title=Project Management Under Risk: Using the Real Options Approach to Evaluate Flexibility in R&D |journal=Management Science |volume=47 |issue=1 |pages=85–101 |doi=10.1287/mnsc.47.1.85.10661 |bibcode=2001ManSc..47...85H }}</ref> Whereas NPV governance primarily manages execution toward an expected outcome, RO governance manages a sequence of decisions through which the organization discovers whether, when, and how to pursue the opportunity.

This flexibility also creates a governance challenge. The probabilistic value of the opportunity can only be realized through successive targeted investments. A high option value should not therefore be interpreted simply as a high likelihood that the project will succeed.  Consequently, effective [[Innovation management|management]] must distinguish between the estimated value of an option and the organizational capability required to attain that value. Research on innovation projects with high uncertainty has identified difficulties in applying real-options reasoning within established management practices.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brasil |first1=Vinicius Chagas |last2=Salerno |first2=Mario Sergio |last3=Gomes |first3=Leonardo Augusto de Vasconcelos |year=2018 |title=Valuation of innovation projects with high uncertainty: Reasons behind the search for real options |journal=Journal of Engineering and Technology Management |volume=49 |pages=109–122 |doi=10.1016/j.jengtecman.2018.08.001}}</ref>

The governance challenges are particularly relevant to [[Three Horizons|Horizon 2]] (H2) development, the intermediate stage between exploratory concepts and projects sufficiently mature for production.<ref name="Sharpe2016">{{cite journal |last=Sharpe |first=Bill |display-authors=et al |date=June 2016 |title=Three Horizons: a pathways practice for transformation |journal=[[Ecology and Society]] |volume=21 |issue=2 |pages=47 |article-number=art47 |doi=10.5751/ES-08388-210247 |bibcode=2016EcSoc..21Tr.47S }}</ref> Research described in ''Leading Horizon 2: Strategies for Transforming Opportunities into Success'' characterizes H2 opportunities as situations in which assumptions about technical feasibility, market potential, and strategic relevance are still developing.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mathews |first1=Scott |last2=Hartwig |first2=Stephanie |date=March 2025 |title=Leading Horizon 2: Strategies for Transforming Opportunities into Success |journal=Preprint |via=ResearchGate |url=https://researchgate.net |access-date=October 2, 2026}}</ref> The study's Opportunity Governance Framework (OGF) combines elements of [[Project portfolio management|innovation portfolio management]],<ref name="Mathews2010">{{cite journal |last1=Mathews |first1=Scott H. |title=Innovation Portfolio Architecture |date=November–December 2010 |journal=Research-Technology Management |volume=53 |issue=6 |pages=30–40 |doi=10.1080/08956308.2010.11657660}}</ref>
<ref name="Mathews2011">{{cite journal |last1=Mathews |first1=Scott H. |title=Innovation Portfolio Architecture—Part 2: Attribute Selection and Valuation |date=September–October 2011 |journal=Research-Technology Management |volume=54 |issue=5 |pages=37–46 |doi=10.5437/08956308X5405005}}</ref> [[systems engineering]], business planning, [[Technology roadmap|road mapping]], and [[choice architecture]] to structure decisions about which opportunities should be pursued, funded, redirected, or abandoned.

Under this approach, failure or abandonment of an opportunity is not necessarily treated as a failure of the governance process. Terminating an opportunity when new evidence has reduced its attractiveness can be an intended governance outcome of staged decision-making. Governance coordinates the initial small, targeted investments that are a justifiable cost of acquiring the necessary information to make a better decision. Governance therefore extends beyond monitoring execution to managing the opportunity, the use of information, reassessing assumptions, and determining when an option should be exercised, modified, or abandoned. In this respect, real-options governance places additional demands on managerial judgment compared with conventional staged project management: the objective is not simply to manage a project toward a predetermined outcome, but to manage a sequence of decisions as uncertainty is progressively resolved. The valuation establishes the potential economic value of flexibility; governance provides the organizational processes through which that flexibility can be evaluated and exercised. AI can strengthen the governance process by structuring relevant information, but ultimate judgment and accountability remains with the organization.

== AI for Real Options ==
Many companies are experimenting with [[artificial intelligence]] (AI) in new-product development, innovation management, and risk management. [[Large language models]] (LLMs) originated as systems that learn patterns in large datasets and estimate probabilities of successive [[Tokenization|tokens]]. In conventional use, they tend to favor statistically likely or “modal” continuations. This makes them effective at synthesizing established knowledge, but can create tension with innovation, where valuable opportunities may be unusual, counterintuitive, or low probability.

This is not a fundamental inability of AI to support innovation; it is a distinction between searching for likely answers and [[Generative AI|generating]] a possibility space for innovation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mariani |first1=Marcello |last2=Dwivedi |first2=Yogesh K. |date=2024 |title=Generative artificial intelligence in innovation management: A preview of future research developments |journal=Journal of Business Research |volume=175 |article-number=114542 |doi=10.1016/j.jbusres.2024.114542 |issn=0148-2963}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gama |first1=Fábio |last2=Magistretti |first2=Stefano |title=Artificial intelligence in innovation management: A review of innovation capabilities and a taxonomy of AI applications |journal=Journal of Product Innovation Management |volume=42 |issue=1 |pages=76–111 |date=January 2025 |doi=10.1111/jpim.12698 |issn=0737-6782 }}</ref> AI systems can be prompted or configured to generate diverse hypotheses, explore counterfactual “what if?” scenarios, and iteratively evaluate alternatives. The aim is to avoid “diversity collapse”—premature convergence on a narrow set of similar ideas.<ref> {{cite journal |last1=Rabby |first1=Gollam |last2=Muhammed |first2=Diyana |last3=Mitra |first3=Prasenjit |last4=Auer |first4=Sören |date=2026 |title=Iterative hypothesis generation for scientific discovery with Monte Carlo self-refining trees |journal=Information Sciences |volume=751 |article-number=123576 |doi=10.1016/j.ins.2026.123576 |issn=0020-0255}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Wang |first1=H. |last2=Shojaee |first2=P. |last3=Meidani |first3=K. |last4=Sun |first4=K. |last5=Hernández-Lobato |first5=J. M. |display-authors=etal |date=2026 |title=Towards Diverse Scientific Hypothesis Search with Large Language Models |eprint=2606.10587 |class=cs.AI}}</ref>

Two simplified prompts illustrate the approach for Opportunity Y, characterized by attributes X1, X2, and X3, for market Z:
*Deliberate divergence:* Generate ten substantially different hypotheses for how Opportunity Y could create value in market Z. Explore conventional, adjacent, unconventional, and low-probability/high-impact possibilities. For each, identify its key assumption, distinguishing feature, and evidence that could support or disprove it. Evaluate the hypotheses only after generating the full set.
*Search toward the tail:* Generate twelve hypotheses and group them as (A) high-probability/conventional, (B) adjacent but non-obvious, (C) low-probability but plausible, and (D) highly unconventional or counterintuitive. For each, describe the assumptions, potential upside, principal uncertainty, and a relatively inexpensive experiment that could test it.
This approach is particularly relevant to real-options (RO) governance, in which relatively small investments can test assumptions before an organization commits more resources. AI-assisted governance also depends on [[standardization|standardizing]]—or “[[canonicalization|canonicalizing]]”—evolving information without erasing uncertainty, disagreement, or changes that may be meaningful signals. Incremental experiments produce new, incomplete, and sometimes contradictory evidence. A governance system should preserve the evidence’s provenance, timing, uncertainty, and contradictions, while reconciling information enough to support comparison and synthesis. Canonicalization is therefore not simply data preparation; it is an ongoing governance activity that maintains a coherent but revisable account of an opportunity.

Within this system, AI could serve four complementary functions: explore opportunities that conventional forecasts or managerial consensus might overlook; integrate evidence, assumptions, dependencies, experiments, and external changes across a portfolio; preserve organizational memory of an option’s strategic intent, decision history, unresolved uncertainties, and rationale as managers change; and compress complex project information into executive briefings that highlight what has changed, what remains uncertain, and which decisions are required.<ref> {{cite journal |last=Kiani |first=Ataullah |date=2025 |title=Artificial intelligence in entrepreneurial project management: a review, framework and research agenda |journal=International Journal of Managing Projects in Business |volume=18 |issue=4–5 |pages=708–720 |doi=10.1108/IJMPB-03-2024-0068}}</ref>

AI need not replace [[Decision intelligence|managerial judgment]] or exercise an option. Its role may instead be an intelligence layer within adaptive governance: exploring possibilities, preserving knowledge, monitoring uncertainty, synthesizing evidence, and identifying where additional information could most improve a decision.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Scherpereel |first=Christopher M. |title=The option-creating institution: A real options perspective on economic organization |journal=Strategic Management Journal |volume=29 |issue=5 |pages=455–470 |year=2008 |doi=10.1002/smj.671}}</ref> RO governance converts that intelligence into staged commitments to continue, pivot, accelerate, or terminate an opportunity. The innovation may therefore lie not in the AI model alone, but in the governance architecture that uses AI to search, learn, and adapt under uncertainty.

== Demand Curve Integration ==
[[File:Demand Price and Cost Curves.jpg|thumb|left|'''Fig. 12 Demand price and cost curves. Point of maximal profitability indicated by triangular markers.''']]
Many early-stage projects find that the dominant unknown values are the first-order range estimates of the major components of operating profits: revenue and manufacturing [[cost of goods sold]] (COGS). In turn the uncertainty about revenue is driven by [[guesstimate]]s of either market demand price or size. Market price and size can be estimated independently, though coupling them together in a [[Demand|market demand]] relationship is a better approach. COGS, the total of cost of product quantity to be sold, is the final component and trends according to an experience or [[Experience curve effects|learning curve]] cost relationship linked to market size. The interplay of these three market elements within a DM Real Options simulation, even with early-stage ranges, can reduce uncertainty for project planning by yielding reasonably narrowed target estimates for product pricing and production size that maximizes potential operating profits and improves option value.

[[File:Differentiated Market.png|thumb|410x300px|left|'''Fig. 13 Left: A highly differentiated airfare market (MCO -- SFO) showing fare amounts paid by passengers (PAX). Right: Cumulative pareto ordering of data illustrating alignment with an inverse lognormal demand curve.''']]

[[File:Operating Profits Graph.jpg|thumb|right|'''Fig. 14 A single instance example (simulation draw) of the three components that form the operating profits graph. The triangular markers indicate a maximum value for operating profit, delineating optimal price, units, and cost values. Yellow rows indicate optimal ranges.''']]

A market price [[demand curve]] graphs the relationship of price to size, or quantity demanded. The [[law of demand]] states there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, or simply as the price decreases product quantity demanded will increase. A second curve, the manufacturing cost graph, models the learning curve effect illustrating the relationship between the quantity of goods produced and the efficiency gains of that production. Fig. 12. Mathematically, the [[Experience curve effects|learning curve]] takes the form of a power function.<ref>[[Experience curve effects#Wright's law unit cost curve|Wright's law:]] <math>C_x = C_1 x^{\log_2 (b)},</math> where <math>C_x</math> is the cost of production the <math>x^{th}</math> unit, <math>C_1</math> is the cost of first unit, and b is the progress ratio. 1-b is the proportion reduction in the unit cost with each doubling in the cumulative production (learning rate). Across many industries estimates of b range from 0.75 to 0.9.  Sometimes <math>C_1</math> can be difficult to estimate, especially in early-stage project planning. Instead, a target production cost is estimated for a future production unit, say <math>C_{30,000}</math> for example. The learning curve formula is then calculated in reverse to estimate <math>C_1.</math></ref>

A demand curve can be realistically modeled using an inverse lognormal distribution which convolves the market price distribution estimate with the market size range.<ref>Demand curve U.S. Patent No. 7,627,495 (issued December 1, 2009).</ref><ref>Typically, market demand price is estimated as a range in normal units, such as $40K - $90K, with a confidence range like 10%-90%. Mathematically assessing a market price by probability, that is percentage increments of market size, requires conversion to lognormal units. Many spreadsheet add-in programs (Oracle’s Crystal Ball, @Risk, etc.), automatically convert confidence ranges of normal mean and standard deviation values to lognormal distributions parameters. Here are the conversion formulas: <math> LogMean=\ln \left( \tfrac{NormMean ^2}{\sqrt {NormStdev ^2 + NormMean ^2}}\right ),</math> and <math>LogStdev=\sqrt {\ln \left (1 + \tfrac {NormStdev ^2}{NormMean ^2} \right )}</math>. The Excel formula for market price by probability increments is expressed as an inverse lognormal function: <math> Lognorm.inv = (probability, LogMean, LogStdev).</math></ref> A demand curve deftly models highly [[Product differentiation|differentiated markets]] which through pricing distinguish selective product or service characteristics such as quality or grade, functional features, and availability, along with quantity sold. Examples are automobiles, shoes, smart phones, and computers. [[Airfare]] markets are highly differentiated where demand pricing and quantity sold are dependent on seasonality, day of week, time of day, routing, sale promotions, and seating or fare class. The airfare demand distribution pattern is well represented with an inverse lognormal distribution as shown in Fig. 13.

Curves for all the above components, market price, size, and COGS, can be simulated with variability to yield an optimal operating profit input for the real option calculation (Fig. 14). For example, the simulation results represented in Fig. 15. indicate ranges for price and unit quantity that potentially will maximize profitability. Extracted from these first-order range estimates, a selection of the peak (frequency) values identifies a significantly narrowed spread of promising estimates. Knowing these optimal value spreads substantially reduces uncertainty and provides a better, more targeted set of parameters from which to confidently base innovation development plans and option value.

[[File:Optimal Ranges to Maximize Profitability.jpg|thumb|410x300px|center|'''Fig. 15 Optimal ranges to maximize profitability. Left: Price $56K - $62K. Right: Units 120K - 150K. Result is 85%+ improved estimate.''']]

== Comparison to other methods ==
The [[fuzzy pay-off method for real option valuation]], created in 2009, provides another accessible approach to real option valuation. Though each use differing mathematical methods (Fuzzy: [[fuzzy logic]]; DM: numerical simulation and geometry) the underlying principal is strikingly similar: the likelihood of a positive payoff. Separately examining the two factors (possibility/probability, and positive payoff) demonstrates this similarity. [[File:Ratio of areas is proportional to the probability.png|thumb|right|128x128px|'''Fig. 16 Ratio of areas is proportional to the probability.''']]

The possibility function for the fuzzy pay-off is <math> \tfrac{A(Pos)}{A(Pos)+A(Neg)} </math>. A simple interpretation is the [[Proportionality (mathematics)|proportionality]] [[ratio]] of the positive area of the fuzzy NPV over the total area of the fuzzy NPV. The probability of the project payoff for the DM Range Option is proportional to the area (CDF) of the positive distribution relative to the complete distribution. This is computed as <math> \tfrac{\left ( b-X_0 \right)^2}{\left [ \left ( b-a \right)\left(b-m\right ) \right ]}.</math> In each the ratios of the areas compute to the same possibility/probability value. The positive payoff of fuzzy pay-off simply is the mean of the positive area of the fuzzy NPV, or <math> E [A^+]</math>. Likewise, the positive payoff for the DM Range Option is the mean of the right tail (''MT''), or <math> \tfrac {\left (2X_0+b \right)}{3} </math> less the strike price <math> X_0 </math> This insight to the mechanics of the two methods illustrates not only their similarity but also their equivalency.

In a 2016 article in the ''[[Advances in Decision Sciences]]'' journal, researchers from the [[Lappeenranta University of Technology]] School of Business and Management compared the DM Method to the [[fuzzy pay-off method for real option valuation]] and noted that while the valuation results were similar, the fuzzy pay-off one was more robust in some conditions.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1155/2016/7836784 | title=Comparison of the Datar-Mathews Method and the Fuzzy Pay-Off Method through Numerical Results | journal=Advances in Decision Sciences | date=12 October 2016 | volume=2016 | last1=Mariia | first1=Kozlova | last2=Mikael | first2=Collan | last3=Pasi | first3=Luukka | pages=1–7 | doi-access=free }}</ref> In some comparative cases, the Datar-Mathews Method has a significant advantage in that it is easier to operate and connects NPV valuation and scenario analysis with Monte Carlo simulation (or geometry) technique thus greatly improving intuition in the usage of real options methods in managerial decision and explanation to third parties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Loukianova |first1=Anna |last2=Nikulin |first2=Egor |last3=Vedernikov |first3=Andrey |title=Valuing synergies in strategic mergers and acquisitions using the real options approach |journal=Investment Management and Financial Innovations |date=12 May 2017 |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=236–247 |doi=10.21511/imfi.14(1-1).2017.10|doi-access=free }}</ref> Through its simulation interface, the Datar-Mathews Method easily accommodates multiple and sometimes correlated cash flow scenarios, including dynamic programming, typical of complex projects, such as aerospace, that are difficult to model using fuzzy sets.<ref>{{cite thesis |last=Schachter |first=Jonathan A. Schachter |date= 2016 |title=A Real Options Approach to Valuing Flexibility in Demand-Side Response Operations and Investments under Uncertainty |type=PhD |publisher=The University of Manchester |url=https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/theses/a-real-options-approach-to-valuing-flexibility-in-demandside-response-operations-and-investments-under-uncertainty(ecde4f40-5e42-4223-b347-fc05ea3ce4f4).html |access-date=2016-08-01}}</ref>

== DM Method and Prospect Theory ==

Real options are about objectively valuing [[innovation]] opportunities. Vexingly, these opportunities, evanescent and seemingly risky, are often comprehended subjectively. However, both the objective valuation mechanism and the subjective interpretation of results are often misunderstood leading to investment reluctance and potentially undervaluing opportunities.

The DM real option employs the objective valuation formula <math>C_0 = E [\max (...,{\color {red} 0)}],</math> where <math>\color {red} 0</math> is the default threshold when it is economically [[rationality|rational]] to terminate (abandon) an opportunity event. If a simulation event (‘draw’) calculates a negative outcome (i.e., <math> [ \tilde S_T e^{-Rt} \leq \tilde X_T e^{-rt} ],</math> operating profits less than launch costs), then that event outcome should be rationally cut, or terminated, recording a <math>\color {red} 0</math> residual. Only net positive economic outcomes <math> [ \tilde S_T e^{-Rt} > \tilde X_T e^{-rt} ]</math> are tallied. This operation leaves the misperception of ‘the odds being stacked’ favoring only positive outcomes seemingly resulting in an abnormally high valuation. However, the <math>E</math> of the formula <math>C_0 = E [\max (...,0)]</math> mathematically calculates the correct option value by adjusting these positive outcomes according to their likelihood, i.e., probability of a success (POS).<ref>Contrast real option valuation with the much lower valuation of an NPV calculation which results from summing all operating profits and launch costs, including negative outcomes, to derive a one-time average value.</ref>
 
The actual DM formula is <math>C_0 = E [\max (...,{\color {red} ?})],</math> where the threshold <math>\color {red} ?</math> (‘floor’) can assume any value (or alternative formula) including the default <math>\color {red} 0</math>. Using a threshold other than <math>\color {red} 0</math> transforms the formula into a hurdle-weighted option variation. The result is no longer equivalent to the value of a financial option.
[[File:Low probability, high value outcomes.jpg|alt=Low probability, high value outcomes (red circle)|thumb|'''Fig. 17 Low probability, high value outcomes (red circle).''']]
Much of the perceived ''high'' value of a real option valuation is disproportionately located in the far-right end of the tail of the simulation distribution, an area of low probability but high value outcomes. The option valuation reflects the potential opportunity value if the various outcome assumptions are validated. Targeted, incremental investments can validate these low probability assumptions. If not, replace the assumptions with proven ‘plausible’ elements, then recalculate the value based on new learnings.

The subjective undervaluation of real options partially can be explained by [[behavioral sciences]]. An innovation investor may perceive the initial investments to be potentially at a loss, particularly if the POS is low. [[Daniel Kahneman|Kahneman]] and Tversky's [[Prospect theory]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kahneman |first1=Daniel |last2=Tversky |first2=Amos |date=March 1979 |title=Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision Under Risk |journal=Econometrica |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=263–291|doi=10.2307/1914185 |jstor=1914185 }}</ref> proclaims that losses are perceived to have an impact more than twice that of gains for the same value.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kahneman |first1=Daniel |last2=Tversky |first2=Amos |date=1992 |title=Advances in prospect theory: Cumulative representation of uncertainty |journal=Journal of Risk and Uncertainty |volume=5 |issue=4 |pages=297–323|doi=10.1007/BF00122574 }}</ref><ref>In behavioral equilibrium <math> gains \approxeq 2 \times losses.</math> Translating this finding to innovation investments, if <math> gains = benefits - investments</math> and perceived <math> losses = investments \ at \ risk,</math> then <math>benefits \approx 3 \times investments.</math> An individual would typically wager only about $33 on a coin flip $100 payoff bet for a total gain of $67.</ref> The result is the [[loss aversion|loss averse]] investor will subjectively undervalue the opportunity, and therefore the investment, despite the objective and financially accurate real option valuation. The pursuit of Prospect Theory has recently led to the related fields of [[behavioral economics]] and [[behavioral economics#behavioral finance|behavioral finance]].

[[Regret (decision theory)|Regret]] aversion, another behavioral science observation, occurs when an unfounded decision is made to avoid regretting a future outcome. For example, a regret-averse investor decides to invest in a relatively ‘sure bet’ but smaller payoff opportunity relative to an alternative with a significantly higher but presumably uncertain payoff. The regret aversion phenomenon is closely aligned with [[ambiguity aversion|uncertainty aversion]] (certainty bias), where the unknown aspects of the innovation opportunity (i.e., newness, lack of control) are rationalized as a hurdle to further investments. The consequences of loss- and regret-averse decision-making are parsimonious investments and underfunding (‘undervaluing’) of promising early-stage innovation opportunities.

A savvy investor can overcome the perceived mis-valuation of an option price. Loss aversion registers significantly high when the entire option value is interpreted as investment risk. This emotional response fails to consider that the initial early-stage investments are only a fraction of the entire option value, necessarily targeted to validate the most salient assumptions. Similarly regret aversion should not be misconceived as [[risk aversion (psychology)|risk aversion]] because the exposure of small early-stage investments is usually not material. Instead, these initial investments carefully probe the opportunity's core value while providing a sense of control over an otherwise uncertain outcome. Regret is minimized by the realization that the opportunity development can be terminated if the assumption outcomes are not promising. The investment funds expended are prudently applied only to investigate a promising opportunity, and, in return, are enhanced by the acquired knowledge.

Since individuals are prone to [[cognitive bias]]es, various intervention strategies are designed to reduce them including expert review along with bias and [[Naïve realism (psychology)|naïve realism]] awareness.<ref name="Fischhoff1982">{{cite book |last1=Fischhoff |first1=Baruch |date=1982 |title=Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases |editor1-last=Kahneman |editor1-first=Daniel |editor2-last=Slovic |editor2-first=Paul |editor3-last=Tversky |editor3-first=Amos |chapter=Debiasing |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |pages=422–444 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511809477.032 |isbn=978-0-521-28414-1 }}</ref>
 A phenomenon termed “[[bias blind spot]]” succinctly describes an individual's unconscious susceptibility to biases.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter=Claims and denials of bias and their implications for policy |last1=Pronin |first1=Emily |last2=Schmidt |first2=K. |date=2013 |title=The behavioral foundations of public policy |publisher=Princeton University Press  |pages=195–216}}</ref> This [[fundamental attribution error]] remains subconsciously hidden by an [[introspection illusion|illusion of self-introspection]], i.e., that we believe, falsely, we have access to our inner intentions or motivations. [[Bias#Implicit bias|Biases]] may be post hoc rationalized away, but nonetheless impact decision-making. To counteract biases, it is insufficient simply be aware of their characteristics, but necessary also to become educated of one's own introspection illusion.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Pronin |first=Emily |date=2009 |title=Advances in Experimental Social Psychology |chapter=Chapter 1: The Introspection Illusion |series=<!-- Advances in Experimental Social Psychology --> |publisher=Academic Press |volume=41 |pages=1–67 |doi=10.1016/S0065-2601(08)00401-2 |isbn=978-0-12-374472-2 |issn=0065-2601}}</ref>

{{Short description|American psychiatric classification}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=February 2024}}
{{Use American English|date=February 2024}}
[[File:DiagnosticAndStatisticalManualOfMentalDisorders.jpg|thumb|1952 edition of the DSM (DSM-I)]]

The '''''Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders''''' ('''''DSM'''''; latest edition: ''[[DSM-5-TR]]'', published in March 2022) is a publication by the [[American Psychiatric Association]] (APA) for the [[classification of mental disorders]] using a common language and standard criteria. It is an internationally accepted manual on the diagnosis and treatment of mental disorders, though it may be used in conjunction with other (international) classification documents. Other commonly used principal guides of psychiatry include the [[International Classification of Diseases]] (ICD), [[Chinese Classification of Mental Disorders]] (CCMD), and the ''[[Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual]]''. However, not all providers rely on the DSM-5 as a guide, since the ICD's mental disorder diagnoses are used around the world,<ref name ="Do mental health professionals use diagnostic classifications the way we think they do? A global survey">{{Cite journal|vauthors=First M, Rebello T, Keeley J, Bhargava R, Dai Y, Kulygina M, Matsumoto C, Robles R, Stona A, Reed G | display-authors = 3| title=Do mental health professionals use diagnostic classifications the way we think they do? A global survey|journal=World Psychiatry |volume=17|issue=2|pages= 187–195|pmid = 29856559| date = June 2018 | doi=10.1002/wps.20525|pmc= 5980454 }}</ref> and scientific studies often measure changes in symptom scale scores rather than changes in DSM-5 criteria to determine the real-world effects of mental health interventions.<ref name = "Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis">{{Cite journal|vauthors = Cipriani A, Furukawa TA, Salanti G, Chaimani A, Atkinson LZ, Ogawa Y, Leucht S, Ruhe HG, Turner EH, Higgins JP, Egger M, Takeshima N, Hayasaka Y, Imai H, Shinohara K, Tajika A, Ioannidis JP, Geddes JR | display-authors = 3| title = Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis | journal = [[The Lancet]] | date = 7 April 2018 | volume = 391 | issue = 10128 | pages = 1357–1366 | doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(17)32802-7 | pmid = 29477251 | pmc = 5889788 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors= Bandelow B, Reitt M, Röver C, Michaelis S, Görlich Y, Wedekind D | display-authors = 3| journal= International Clinical Psychopharmacology | title=Efficacy of treatments for anxiety disorders: a meta-analysis | volume=30 | issue=4 | pages=183–192 | date= July 2015 | doi=10.1097/YIC.0000000000000078| pmid= 25932596 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | vauthors= Schneider-Thoma J, Chalkou K, Dörries C, Bighelli I, Ceraso A, Huhn M, Siafis S, Davis JM, Cipriani A, Furukawa TA, Salanti G, Leucht S | journal=Lancet | display-authors = 3| title=Comparative efficacy and tolerability of 32 oral and
